vignette:
He is sixty-eight now, a seasoned European politician who has spent most of his adult life in public rooms: council chambers, campaign halls, television studios, parliamentary corridors where people clap him on the shoulder and expect him to know what to say. Before the accident, he thinks of himself as someone who moved through pressure almost effortlessly. He liked the theater of politics, the quick thinking, the negotiation, the physical stamina of long days and late-night votes. His wife used to joke that he was most relaxed when three crises were unfolding at once.

The accident happens on a winter evening five years ago, after a regional party meeting in a provincial city. He is being driven back along a dark motorway in heavy rain. He remembers looking down at briefing papers under the dim car light, rehearsing lines for a morning interview, when he feels the sudden sickening loss of control. There is the shriek of tires, a violent sideways pull, headlights rushing toward him from the opposite lane, and then the impact. Metal folds around him. Glass bursts across his face and lap. For a few seconds, maybe longer, he is trapped in a silence that does not feel real, followed by the smell of fuel and hot rubber. He cannot move his left leg. He is sure the car will catch fire. He hears the driver making a sound he cannot identify at first, then realizes it is screaming.

What remains most vivid is not the pain but the certainty that he is about to die while fully conscious. He remembers trying to unbuckle himself with shaking hands that no longer seem to belong to him. He remembers thinking of his wife not sentimentally but with startling practical clarity-who would call her, how she would hear, what unfinished things he had left in motion. When emergency workers finally pull him out, he feels humiliated by his own terror. Even on the roadside, soaked and shivering under foil blankets, he apologizes for "making a fuss."

His injuries heal better than anyone first expects. He returns to public life within months, helped along by aides, party colleagues, and his own insistence that he is fortunate. He tells the story as others want to hear it: terrible crash, lucky escape, onward. He gives interviews from a cane-backed chair and smiles grimly about resilience. What he does not say is that from the first week home, sleep becomes a place of ambush. He wakes drenched, his heart hammering, hearing again the crunch of metal and seeing those headlights aimed at him. Sometimes he wakes with his hands clawing at the bedsheets as if trying to free himself from twisted seatbelts. His wife touches his shoulder and he jerks away before he knows where he is.

At first he assumes this will pass. Instead, his world begins quietly to shrink. He no longer reads in the back seat of a moving car. Then he stops sitting in the back seat altogether, insisting on the front so he can monitor the road. Soon even short drives on wet evenings leave him gripping the armrest, jaw clenched, scanning every oncoming vehicle. If a truck drifts slightly within its lane, his chest tightens and his breath goes shallow. More than once he has barked at drivers to slow down or pull over, then sat rigid with embarrassment, pretending irritation rather than fear.

His work changes with him. In debate, he is still articulate, but staff notice he startles at slammed doors and raised voices. During sessions in parliament, the sudden scrape of chairs can send a jolt through him so intense that he loses the thread of discussion. He becomes more controlling, less patient, furious over small logistical errors. He tells himself he is simply less tolerant of incompetence with age, but privately he knows something raw lives just under the surface. He cannot bear last-minute route changes. He checks weather reports obsessively before travel. If rain is forecast, his mood darkens hours in advance.

He avoids the motorway where the crash occurred, although detouring adds considerable time. He has never visited the site. When constituents speak to him about road safety campaigns, he feels his throat close. Publicly, he can stand at a podium and speak about infrastructure, fatalities, and legislative urgency in polished, measured language. Privately, actual images intrude without warning: shattered glass in his mouth, the smell of petrol, the sensation of being pinned and waiting to burn. These moments come while he is shaving, while reviewing policy notes, while sitting across from a journalist asking an unrelated question. He blinks and continues, but for a second he is no longer in the present.

At home, his wife sees the cost most clearly. He is less available, though rarely absent in body. He sits through dinner with one ear tuned to traffic outside. He used to enjoy spontaneous weekend trips; now he wants detailed departure times, mapped routes, assurances about roads and weather. She says he is always braced. He knows she is right. The world feels unpredictably dangerous in a way it never did before, and he resents that he, of all people, cannot seem to master it.

What troubles him most is the split between his public self and private experience. Voters still see composure, authority, confidence. He still delivers speeches about stability in uncertain times. Yet much of each day is organized around not feeling what he felt that night in the car. He is tired from the effort of containing it-tired from poor sleep, from vigilance, from the constant small calculations required to keep panic from overtaking him. He says, with a mixture of shame and disbelief, that surviving the crash was straightforward compared with living afterward, when nothing is visibly broken and yet he never again feels entirely safe.
